fields.Front: List the eleven advantages of OOP covered in Week 1.
fields.Back: Modularity, Reusability, Encapsulation, Maintainability, Extensibility, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Team Collaboration, Security and Access Control, Scaling, Debugging and Testing.
Breaking a system into smaller, self-contained classes each performing a specific function; e.g., ShoppingCart, Order, Payment developed independently.
Base class Vehicle reused for Car, Bike, Truck; reuse base functionality and extend where needed.
BankAccount exposes deposit() and withdraw() but keeps balance private, protecting state from outside interference.

fields.Front: Advantage: Maintainability. What concept and example?
fields.Back: Separation of concerns: each class handles a specific part; a bug in Payment can be fixed without affecting ShoppingCart or Order.

fields.Front: Advantage: Extensibility. Which principle is it tied to?
fields.Back: The Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification; add new classes/methods without changing existing code.

fields.Text: The polymorphism advantage example: a `{{c1::PaymentMethod}} interface with implementations CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, and CryptoPayment`; new payment types are added without changing processing logic.

fields.Back: Game base class Character with health, strength, move(), attack(); Warrior and Mage inherit and add unique abilities.
Clearly defined interfaces let one team build the User class while another builds Transaction.

fields.Front: Advantage: Security and Access Control. Example?
fields.Back: A BankTransaction class limits access to sensitive methods (e.g., transfers) based on user roles using access modifiers.
Microservices: UserService, PaymentService as objects with well-defined interfaces; PaymentService can be scaled independently.
Classes are self-contained units testable in isolation via mock objects or dependency injection; test Order by mocking Payment and Shipping.

fields.Text: Extensibility in OOP means being open for {{c1::extension}} but closed for {{c2::modification}} (the Open/Closed Principle).
Maintainability in OOP relies on {{c1::separation of concerns}}: each class is responsible for a specific part of the system.
